name: Blockchain Generations
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Generations of Blockchain: A Rough Map, Not a Law
lesson.summary: Industry commentary often sorts blockchain development into loose generations, from Bitcoin's payments focus to Ethereum's programmability to later scaling and interoperability efforts, but the framing is informal and should be read with some skepticism.
lesson.body:
Industry commentary often describes blockchain's development in terms of generations: first generation, second generation, and so on. It is worth being upfront that this is an informal narrative used for teaching and marketing purposes, not a rigorous technical standard with fixed criteria that any authority enforces. Used carefully, it is a helpful map of how the field's priorities shifted over time; used carelessly, it turns into a ranking system that projects apply to themselves to sound more advanced than competitors.

The first generation label is usually applied to Bitcoin, covered two chapters back. Its contribution was proving that decentralized, trust minimized digital money could actually work at scale among strangers, using proof of work and a deliberately narrow, non-programmable design focused on payments and value transfer. Nothing before Bitcoin had demonstrated this combination working in practice, which is why it anchors the starting point of the generational story.

The second generation label centers on Ethereum, covered in the previous chapter. Its contribution was generalizing the same underlying structure, a chain of cryptographically linked blocks secured by decentralized consensus, into a programmable platform through smart contracts and the Ethereum Virtual Machine. This reframed blockchain from being purely a payments system into being a form of infrastructure that developers could build arbitrary applications on top of, which is the shift that produced the broader ecosystem of decentralized applications built after Bitcoin's initial model.

A third generation label gets applied, often by the projects making the claim about themselves, to networks attempting to address problems that became visible once the first two generations were used at real scale: limited transaction throughput and high fees during periods of heavy demand, and difficulty getting separate blockchains to communicate or exchange value with each other, usually called interoperability. Projects pursuing these goals have experimented with alternative consensus designs, sharding approaches that split transaction processing across parallel groups, and layered architectures that handle most activity off the main chain. Because this label is self applied inconsistently and frequently used as marketing language rather than a technical classification anyone certifies, it deserves real skepticism; calling a network third generation is a claim about intent, not proof of technical superiority or security.

The most useful way to hold this framework is as a rough memory aid for how priorities evolved, from proving decentralized money could work, to making blockchains programmable, to addressing scale and interoperability at the edges, rather than as a strict ladder every project climbs in order. Plenty of ideas associated with later generations were proposed or discussed before Ethereum even launched, and plenty of networks blend concerns from multiple generations at once. The generations story is a starting point for orientation, not a scoreboard.
